readerTitle: Before you buy the boxes: testing a meal-kit idea in a grocery store
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식료품점의 밀키트, 냉장 배송 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 아이디어 검증은 가장 치명적인 가정 하나를 골라, 장비를 사기 전에 손으로 직접 해 보며 확인하는 것이다.
misconception: 밀키트 같은 새 상품은 포장 라인, 브랜드 박스, 주문 앱부터 갖춰야 제대로 시험해 볼 수 있다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 (CUS-04-01 가장 위험한 가정, CUS-04-04 먼저 손으로 해 보기)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 키트 가격 $30, 같은 재료를 매장 진열대에서 사면 약 $22라는 가정입니다. 차액 $8가 고객이 '편리함'에 내는 돈입니다.
손 포장 계산: 키트 20개 포장에 3시간, 시급 $18 가정 → $54 ÷ 20 = 키트당 $2.70. 20개 중 14개 판매 = 70%. 다음 주 재구매 6명 = 구매자 14명 중 약 43%.
식품 위생·포장 관련 규정은 나라와 지역마다 다르므로 카드에서는 '현지 규정을 확인하라'는 일반적인 문장만 쓰고 구체적 법률 조언은 하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Before you buy the boxes: testing a meal-kit idea in a grocery store
body: Maya runs a neighborhood grocery store. Busy parents keep asking her what to cook tonight. She has an idea: weekly meal kits, with every ingredient for three dinners in one bag.
A supplier is already quoting her for a packing table, 1,000 branded boxes and a simple ordering app. Before she signs, let's use two ideas from this unit.

image.label: A grocery owner looking at a stack of empty branded boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 식료품점 계산대 옆, 주인이 아직 비어 있는 새 밀키트 박스 더미를 바라보며 고민하는 장면. 박스에는 가상의 단순한 무늬만, 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya check first?
body: Maya has a week and a small budget. Many things must go right: demand, price, freshness, packing time, recipes.

options.text: Design the box and the ordering app, since customers judge by looks
options.feedback: Good design helps later. But it spends money on the part least likely to sink the idea, before she knows anyone will pay.

options.text: Survey shoppers on whether they'd buy meal kits
options.feedback: Cheap and quick. But saying yes costs shoppers nothing, so a survey can't tell her whether they'll actually pay.

options.text: List her assumptions and test the one that would kill the idea if it's wrong
options.feedback: This is **your riskiest assumption** at work. Find the belief the whole plan rests on, and test that before anything else.

cards.title: Which belief holds up the whole plan?
body: Most of these can be fixed if they go wrong. The last one can't. If shoppers won't pay **$30 for a bag they could fill themselves for about $22**, nothing else matters.

breakdown.label: Shoppers pay $8 extra for convenience
breakdown.detail: The same items sit one aisle away

cards.title: How should Maya test it this week?
body: She wants to know if shoppers will really pay $30, not just say they would.

options.text: Order the packing table and 1,000 boxes, then launch properly
options.feedback: She'd learn the answer, but only after paying for everything. If shoppers say no, the boxes become a storage problem.

options.text: Hand-pack 20 kits in paper bags with a printed recipe card and sell them at the register for $30
options.feedback: This is **doing it by hand first**. Real kits, real price, real buyers, almost no equipment. She also learns what packing really takes.

options.text: Put up a "Meal kits coming soon" sign with a sign-up sheet
options.feedback: It shows interest for nearly nothing. But a name on a sheet isn't $30 at the register, and price is the assumption she most needs to test.

cards.softwareNote: Software founders do the same thing. Before building an automated feature, they deliver the result by hand behind a simple form, then build only what users keep coming back for.

cards.title: 14 kits sold, and one surprise.
body: Maya sold 14 of her 20 kits at full price. Her riskiest assumption survived its first real test.
Doing it by hand also showed her something no quote could. Packing took her staff **3 hours**. At $18 an hour, that's $2.70 a kit, a cost she hadn't counted.
The next week, 6 of the 14 buyers came back. That repeat number told her more than the first sale.

image.label: Paper-bag kits by a register, with a tally sheet
image.brief: 계산대 옆 선반에 손으로 포장한 종이봉투 밀키트들과 레시피 카드. 옆에 손글씨 표: "Packed 20 / Sold 14 / Came back 6". 따뜻한 매장 조명, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Hand-made tests can flatter you.
body: Twenty kits packed with care by the owner won't match 500 packed in a rush. Early buyers may also be curious regulars who would buy anything Maya tried.
So judge by repeat purchases over several weeks, not first-week sales. And count the hand costs honestly, because they show what scaling up must fix.
Food also carries rules on handling and labeling. Check local requirements before selling, even in a small test.

cards.title: Now it's a cold-chain delivery company.
body: You run a refrigerated trucking company serving supermarkets. You think restaurants would pay for small, early-morning deliveries of chilled goods.
A dealer offers you five small refrigerated vans on a three-year lease. What do you do?

options.text: Lease the vans so the service looks reliable from day one
options.feedback: Reliable, yes. But you've locked in three years of cost before learning whether restaurants will pay your price for small drops.

options.text: Rent one van for a month and run a route for five restaurants yourself, at the real price
options.feedback: You test **your riskiest assumption**, that restaurants will pay, by **doing it by hand first**. You also learn real drop times and loading problems.

options.text: Ask your supermarket clients' suppliers whether restaurants need this
options.feedback: They may know the market well. But secondhand opinions can't tell you whether restaurant owners will sign and pay.

cards.title: Test the belief that could sink you, by hand, before you buy the equipment.
body: Two ideas did the work in this lesson:
list: **Your riskiest assumption:** shoppers must pay extra for convenience, so test that first
**Doing it by hand first:** 20 paper bags and one rented van taught more than any quote
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down the one belief your next idea can't survive without. Then plan the smallest hand-run test of it at the real price.
